title: Using Norwegian -ende Forms Without Overusing English -ing
goal: Recognize and use Norwegian present participles as invariable adjective-like and adverb-like forms, and replace mechanical English -ing translations with more natural Norwegian structures.

objectives.statement: Recognize and use Norwegian present participles as invariable adjective-like and adverb-like forms, and replace mechanical English -ing translations with more natural Norwegian structures.

spans.value: Ingrid and Jonas are viewing an apartment with Mari, the estate agent. The building is quiet, but several small details make them wonder what living there would be like.

spans.value: The important question is therefore not simply, “How do I translate -ing?” It is, “What job is the English -ing form doing, and what sounds natural in Norwegian?”

The present participle presents an activity, reaction, or state as a characteristic or accompanying circumstance. It does not by itself tell us when the action happens. Time comes from the surrounding sentence.

sections.title: When a relative clause sounds more natural

spans.value: An English noun phrase with -ing can sometimes use a Norwegian present participle:
However, Norwegian often prefers a relative clause with
when the English phrase identifies a person or group by what they regularly do or where they live.

no.value: De som bor over dere, er et eldre par.

en.value: The people living above you are an older couple.

spans.value: in formal language, where it means the residents. In ordinary conversation, however,

no.value: Folk som jobber hjemmefra, trenger ofte et rolig rom.

en.value: People working from home often need a quiet room.

no.value: Studentene som venter utenfor, skal på visning.

en.value: The students waiting outside are going to the viewing.

no.value: Kvinnen som snakker med Mari, er Ingrid.

en.value: The woman speaking with Mari is Ingrid.

spans.value: A present participle may sound compressed, descriptive, literary, or formal where a relative clause sounds clearer and more conversational.
Compare these two ways of viewing the same scene:

en.value: I saw a man who was carrying a large box.

no.value: Jeg så en mann bærende på en stor eske.

en.value: I saw a man carrying a large box.

sections.title: Adverb-like use: an accompanying action or manner

spans.value: A present participle can also be
. It then describes how someone moves, arrives, reacts, speaks, or performs another action.

no.value: Naboen kom bærende på en stor eske.

en.value: The neighbour came carrying a large box.

spans.value: The main event is his arrival.
describes his condition or accompanying activity when he arrived.
This pattern is particularly common with movement and position:

en.value: She came cycling down the hill.

no.value: Barna løp leende ut i hagen.

en.value: The children ran laughing into the garden.

no.value: Han gikk haltende bort til bilen.

en.value: He walked limping over to the car.
We remained standing outside the door.

no.value: De ble sittende og snakke etter møtet.

en.value: They remained sitting and talking after the meeting.

spans.value: Present participles can also describe manner:

en.value: Ingrid nodded to Mari with a smile.

spans.value: These sentences do not use the participle to create an English-style progressive tense. The sentence already has a main verb:
. The participle adds an accompanying action, posture, expression, or manner.

en.value: Jonas came running to the bus.

spans.value: The first sentence presents running as the main action. The second presents arrival or movement toward the scene as the main event and running as the manner.
In the first sentence, smiling is the main action. In the second, answering is the main action, while

Norwegian normally uses an ordinary present-tense verb:

Use the ordinary present or past tense when the activity itself is the main statement:

en.value: I am waiting for the bus.

no.value: Jeg ventet på bussen da hun ringte.

en.value: I was waiting for the bus when she called.

spans.value: form when it describes a noun or accompanies another main event:

no.value: De ventende passasjerene så på klokka.

en.value: The waiting passengers looked at the clock.
She came running to the bus stop.

sections.title: Other English -ing forms often need other Norwegian structures

spans.value: English -ing appears in several grammatical jobs. Norwegian chooses a structure according to meaning.
An activity as a general idea
English can make an activity the subject of a sentence with an -ing form: Cycling is good exercise.

no.value: Det er god trening å sykle.
Å lese kontrakten nøye er viktig.

en.value: Reading the contract carefully is important.

no.value: Det er dyrt å bo alene.

spans.value: Two events happening at the same time
English can begin with an -ing phrase: Walking home, Ingrid called Jonas.

no.value: Mens Ingrid gikk hjem, ringte hun Jonas.

en.value: While Ingrid was walking home, she called Jonas.

no.value: På vei hjem ringte Ingrid til Jonas.

en.value: On her way home, Ingrid called Jonas.

no.value: Gående hjemover tenkte Ingrid på leiligheten.

en.value: Walking home, Ingrid thought about the apartment.

spans.value: may also fit the intended meaning:

no.value: På vei hjem ringte Ingrid til Jonas.

en.value: On her way home, Ingrid called Jonas.

spans.value: A present participle is possible in some descriptive contexts, but it can sound more written or compressed:

no.value: Gående hjemover tenkte Ingrid på leiligheten.

en.value: Walking home, Ingrid thought about the apartment.

spans.value: : You open the door by pressing the green button.

no.value: Du åpner døra ved å trykke på den grønne knappen.

en.value: You open the door by pressing the green button.

no.value: De sparer penger ved å dele på utgiftene.

en.value: They save money by sharing the expenses.

spans.value: form is not the automatic solution.
When you meet an English -ing form, ask what it does:

items.value: If it naturally describes a noun, an invariable Norwegian
-ende
form may fit.
If it adds manner or an accompanying action to a main event, an adverb-like
-ende
form may fit.
If it is the main activity in progress, use a finite Norwegian verb.
If it identifies people by what they do, a relative clause with
som
is often natural.
If it names an activity in general, use an infinitive.
If it means while doing something or by doing something, use a clause or an infinitive structure that expresses that relationship clearly.

spans.value: After the viewing, Ingrid and Jonas sit in a café and discuss the apartment.

blocks.translation: What did you think of the apartment?

spans.value: Jeg likte den. Selv den pipende røykvarsleren var ikke så ille.

blocks.translation: I liked it. Even the beeping smoke alarm wasn’t so bad.

spans.value: Jeg tenker fortsatt på vaktmesteren som kom løpende.

blocks.translation: I’m still thinking about the caretaker who came running.

spans.value: Han kom bærende på alle de verktøyene og så ganske stresset ut.

blocks.translation: He came carrying all those tools and looked quite stressed.

spans.value: Hva med folkene som bor i etasjen over?

blocks.translation: What about the people living on the floor above?

spans.value: De virker hyggelige. Og barnebarnet deres sov rolig da vi var der.

blocks.translation: They seem pleasant. And their grandchild was sleeping peacefully while we were there.

spans.value: Skal vi legge inn et tilbud?
Ja. Men først må vi lese den gjeldende salgsoppgaven nøye.

blocks.translation: Yes. But first we need to read the current sales prospectus carefully.

A child is sleeping on a bench, passengers are waiting under the departure board, and a conductor comes running along the platform while speaking on the phone. Jonas is checking the train times. Ingrid buys coffee by using a machine.

Choose the natural everyday Norwegian reformulation. The English meaning identifies the people by where they live, so score the structural choice between a relative clause and a compressed participle phrase.

options.text: De som bor i etasjen over, er et eldre par.
options.why: A relative clause is the usual conversational choice when people are identified by where they live.

options.text: De boende i etasjen over er et eldre par.
options.why: De boende is a formal or compressed expression; the relative clause is more natural in this everyday context.

prompt.value: Write four short Norwegian sentences, one for each numbered meaning. Use a different natural structure for each: (1) during an apartment viewing, we noticed a beeping alarm in the hallway; use an invariable -ende form to describe the alarm; (2) Jonas is waiting for the train; use an ordinary finite verb because waiting is the main activity; (3) the people living above us seem pleasant; use a relative clause with som; (4) reading the contract carefully is important; use an infinitive-based structure. Do not translate every English -ing form mechanically as -ende.

payload.judge_prompt: Check all four sentences against the four numbered meanings and report evidence for each criterion. Accept natural lexical and word-order alternatives when they preserve the meaning and required structure. Reject mechanical er plus -ende progressive forms.

Write four short natural Norwegian sentences about Ingrid and Jonas at the railway station, one for each numbered meaning: (1) the waiting passengers look at the clock; use an invariable adjective-like -ende form; (2) a conductor comes running along the platform while speaking on the phone; use an adverb-like -ende form with a finite main verb; (3) Jonas is looking at the train times; use an ordinary finite Norwegian verb, not være plus -ende; (4) Ingrid buys coffee by pressing the green button; use a natural non-participle method structure with ved å plus an infinitive. Do not use -ende as an automatic translation of every English -ing form.
